name: Olga Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the health reporter for the regional public broadcaster's newsroom, so I write for the website and do short pieces for the morning radio bulletin. A normal day starts at seven with the overnight emails from the hospital trust, then I'm on the phone to GPs, care home managers and patients' families. I like the people stories best, the woman waiting fourteen months for a hip operation, that kind of thing. What wears me out is the pay and the fact that I'm doing a specialist job on a junior wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Does anyone at home share the load?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomas, who's a nurse on the children's ward, so between us we know the health system from both ends. We rent a two-bed flat above a dry cleaner's and we split everything down the middle. Neither of us has much saved; there was a boiler repair in the spring that wiped us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to talking about the actual problems in local news, like funding. I've tried it a few times. AI is handy for transcribing interviews, but it's not going to replace a phone call to a scared family. I'd post something like that and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but only partly. Our newsroom's budget gets squeezed every year whatever happens with AI, and there were voluntary redundancies last winter. I'm not sure my post is safe just because the robots didn't turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and use the transcription tool when it saves me an hour. I'd join the union properly, because I've been meaning to for ages and never got round to the form. Tomas and I would try to rebuild the boiler money, maybe a hundred a month into a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A little uneasy, because nothing about this picture fixes how thin things are for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned voluntary redundancies last winter. Who went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of the older producers and a sports reporter. Their work got spread over the rest of us, so I now edit some of my own audio, which I never trained for. Nobody said it was about AI; it was just money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours were cut, what would you and Tomas drop first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, it's an old hatchback we barely use. Tomas works nights sometimes so we'd keep one bus pass and a bike. We'd keep the flat, because finding anything cheaper near the hospital is nearly impossible.

say: We should get back to the **real problem** in local news, which is funding.
AI **transcription** is handy, but it won't replace a phone call to a scared family.
think: She'd feel **relieved**, but the newsroom budget gets squeezed every year regardless.
Last winter's **redundancies** mean her post isn't automatically safe.
do: Keep using the **transcription tool** when it saves an hour, and otherwise carry on.
Finally fill in the **union form** she's been putting off for ages.
Put about **a hundred a month** aside with her partner to rebuild after the boiler bill.
feel: **Mostly steady**, with a little unease because money stays thin.
S0.quote: AI is handy for transcribing interviews, but it's not going to replace a phone call to a scared family.
fieldNote: Her own post looks **safe enough**, but budget cuts keep the shifting ground on her mind.
Partner's **nursing income** gives the household a bit of ballast that others lack.
Uses AI **pragmatically** already, without any excitement about it.

steps.text: Keep reporting health stories and use AI transcription for long interviews
Fill in the union membership form at last
Save a hundred a month in a separate account with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can help newsrooms, but only if the time it saves goes back into real reporting, not into cuts. I'd want the union to have a say in how it's used. I'd be pretty public about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the website side of my job gets thinner fast. A machine will write the hospital waiting-time figures before I've had my coffee. The trust's board papers will go the same way. What's left is the human stories, and I'm not sure management will pay a full salary for those alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a few other newsrooms have shown it works, I'd learn the AI tools properly, especially for data, so I'm the one who can turn a spreadsheet into a story fast. I'd ask my editor for training time in writing. I'd also quietly look at communications jobs at health charities, because they pay a bit more and need people who understand the NHS.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. I can see a path, I just don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned health charities. Would that feel like leaving journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that bothers me. I went into this to hold the health service to account, not to write its press releases. But if the choice is that or not paying rent, I know which way I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would tell me to stop worrying and point out that nurses are short-staffed everywhere. Then he'd say his shifts are already full, so he can't pick up more hours. That's the real limit, there's no slack in either of our jobs.

say: AI should free time for **real reporting**, not be used to make **cuts**.
The **union** needs a say in how newsrooms use these tools.
think: Routine work like **waiting-time figures** and board papers will be machine-written very quickly.
Management may not pay a **full salary** just for the human stories that remain.
do: Learn the **AI data tools** properly once other newsrooms show they work.
Ask her editor in writing for **training time**.
Quietly look at **communications jobs** at health charities.
feel: **Anxious** but not helpless, because she can see a path she doesn't love.
S1.quote: A machine will write the hospital waiting-time figures before I've had my coffee.
fieldNote: Shows her **steady** style: she'd adopt AI once proven elsewhere, not first.
A real **values conflict** about moving into charity communications.
Household has **no slack**: her partner can't take more shifts.

steps.text: Learn AI data tools for turning health statistics into stories
Request paid training time from her editor in writing
Look at communications jobs at regional health charities
Push the union to agree rules on newsroom AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency measures, like a basic income or a jobs guarantee, before people fall through the floor. I'd say public broadcasters especially have a duty to keep journalists, because trust matters more than ever. I'd post that and share every union statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be redundant inside a year of it arriving. My work is almost all thinking work, calls, writing, checking, and AGI does that better and cheaper by 2028. My partner's job is hands-on, so his ward has until about 2031 before robots matter, and that gap would probably keep us afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd try to get on the newsroom's AI team, if there is one, because the people who run the tools are the last to go. I'd cut the car and anything we can. If I lost the job, I'd look at a healthcare assistant course so I could work alongside Tomas for those three years before robots arrive, even though it pays badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. There's a kind of dizziness to two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas's job buys you about three years. What happens at the end of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's what keeps me up. By 2031 the robots come for hands-on work too, maybe even nursing, though I find that hard to picture on a children's ward. I suppose we'd be relying on whatever the government had set up by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would tell me to come home, she lives two hours north in a small town. I'd say thank you and no, not yet. But I'd be thinking about it.

say: We need **emergency measures** like a basic income or jobs guarantee before people fall through.
**Public broadcasters** have a duty to keep journalists, because trust matters more than ever.
think: She'd be **redundant** within a year, since calls, writing and checking are all thinking work.
Her partner's **hands-on** nursing job has until about 2031, and that gap keeps them afloat.
do: Try to join the newsroom's **AI team**, since tool operators are the last to go.
Sell the **car** and cut every extra straight away.
Take a **healthcare assistant** course if laid off, to work through the 3-year robot gap.
feel: **Scared**, with a kind of dizziness at only two years' warning.
S2.quote: My partner's job is hands-on, so his ward has until about 2031 before robots matter, and that gap would probably keep us afloat.
fieldNote: She grasped the **3-year robot gap** at once and built a household plan on it.
Fully expects to **lose her job**, which makes this alarmed despite a calm tone.
The pull of her **mum's offer** shows how near a move feels.

steps.text: Volunteer for the newsroom's AI tools team
Sell the old hatchback and cut all extras
Take a healthcare assistant course after any redundancy
Share union calls for a basic income or jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and governments should use it to plan retraining and protect public interest journalism. I'd want the union pushing the broadcaster to commit to keeping a newsroom. I'd say that publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me move on my own terms instead of being pushed. My job still mostly goes by 2031, because it's thinking work. But I could spend those years building something sturdier, like health data skills that hospitals and councils need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short online course in health data and statistics, the kind you can do in evenings. I'd keep reporting and use AI more for the data stories so I build a portfolio. Tomas and I would try hard to get to two months' savings and maybe give up the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more like I'm planning a hard trip than falling off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait until things are proven. Would five years be enough time to wait and still move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point. I think I'd wait about a year to see who's actually hiring, then commit. Waiting longer than a year would just be fear dressed up as caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bulletin producers, who stitch the radio news together at five in the morning. Their job is all checking and timing, which machines do well. Some of them have kids and mortgages, which I don't, so they'd be in a much worse spot.

say: Five years is a **warning** that governments should use to plan **retraining**.
The broadcaster should commit to **keeping a newsroom**, and the union should push for it.
think: Her reporting job still mostly **goes by 2031**, since it's thinking work.
Five years lets her move on her **own terms** instead of being pushed out.
do: Do an evening course in **health data** and statistics in the first year.
Build a **portfolio** of AI-assisted data stories while still reporting.
Aim for **two months' savings** with her partner, possibly by selling the car.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like planning a hard trip rather than falling.
S3.quote: Waiting longer than a year would just be fear dressed up as caution.
fieldNote: Caught her own **contradiction** about waiting and set herself a one-year limit.
Still expects to **lose the reporting role**, so the mood stays high even with a plan.
Shows **empathy** for older producers with kids and mortgages.

steps.text: Take an evening online course in health data and statistics
Publish AI-assisted health data stories as a portfolio
Build two months of savings with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a real chance to do this fairly, and there's no excuse for leaving people behind. I'd be pushing for public funding for local journalism as a public service, like libraries. I'd post about it and probably write an opinion piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel I could build a proper second career. I'd be thirty-seven, Tomas and I might have kids by then, and I'd want something steady before that. Journalism as I know it will be smaller, but people who understand health systems and data will still be needed somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for two or three years, use AI more and more, and save. Then I'd look at a part-time master's in public health, maybe with an employer paying part. Tomas and I would also hold off deciding about kids until we can see how it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anxious. Ten years is time, and time is the thing we never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How much does this shape that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I'd like. We'd always said thirty or so. With this hanging over us, I think we'd push it back until one of us had a job we trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger reporter starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young reporter to learn data and a specialism, health or courts or planning, not just writing. Writing on its own is the first thing to go. Knowing a field deeply lasts longer.

say: A decade is a **real chance** to do this fairly, with no excuse for leaving people behind.
Local journalism should get **public funding** as a public service, like libraries.
think: Ten years lets her build a **second career** before she's thirty-seven.
People who understand **health systems** and data will still be needed somewhere.
do: Keep reporting for **two or three years** while using AI more and saving.
Apply for a **part-time master's** in public health, ideally partly employer-funded.
Put **children** on hold until one of them has a job they trust.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than anxious, because ten years of time feels rare.
S4.quote: I'd tell a young reporter to learn data and a specialism, health or courts or planning, not just writing.
fieldNote: Long runway lowers her mood, since she sees a **credible path** into public health.
AI is quietly reshaping **family plans**: children pushed back past thirty.
Her advice to young reporters shows **specialism** as her main survival idea.

steps.text: Keep reporting health for two or three more years
Apply for a part-time public health master's
Delay starting a family until one job feels secure
Keep saving monthly towards a three-month cushion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit me before Tomas and we'd have no time to plan around it. What would help is paid retraining with a wage while you do it, and public money for local news so it isn't just whoever can make a profit. Even a guaranteed six months' pay after redundancy would change everything for us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how this lands on couples. My partner Tomas and I sort of hedge each other, his job is hands-on and mine isn't, and that's the only reason I'm not more frightened. A single reporter on my wage wouldn't have that, and I think about them a lot.

headlineQuote: My partner Tomas and I sort of hedge each other, his job is hands-on and mine isn't, and that's the only reason I'm not more frightened.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old health reporter** at a regional public broadcaster, renting with her nurse partner.
She uses AI **now and then** and would adopt it more once other newsrooms prove it works.
She feels **uneasy** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** in the faster AGI pictures, expecting to lose her role.
Her partner's **hands-on** nursing job is the household's hedge, and she plans around the 3-year robot gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would hit her before her partner, leaving no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a wage, and **public money** for local news.
A guaranteed **six months' pay** after redundancy.
